newsitem.title: UK: Using AIDS cocktails pays off say drug companies.
newsitem.headline: Using AIDS cocktails pays off say drug companies.

text.p: Combination therapy using two or more drugs to subdue the HIV virus that causes AIDS may be expensive but it pays in the long run, pharmaceutical companies and doctors said on Monday.
Use of F. Hoffman-La Roche's new protease inhibitor Invirase (saquinavir) with Glaxo-Wellcome's AZT can offset medical costs by $2,000-$5,700 a patient per year, Roche told a Birmingham conference.
"Cost data from eight expensive U.S. hospitals show savings as high as $6,339," Roche said in a statement distributed at the third International Congress on Drug Therapy in HIV Infection.

Doctors have been telling the congress that patients given cocktails of two or three drugs are feeling better, gaining weight and not showing up with opportunistic infections such as pneumonia, Kaposi's sarcoma or cytomegalovirus (CMV).

Jeremy Chancellor of Glaxo-Wellcome told the conference that AIDS patients can cost a state-run healthcare programme -- or an insurer -- 11,285 pounds a year. But he said the drugs offset some of these costs.
"We believe that combination therapy of 3TC (Glaxo's Epivir) with AZT is cost-effective," he said. "We believe that combination therapy should routinely be funded."

Glaxo earlier announced that dual therapy with AZT and 3TC cut AIDS deaths by up to 53 percent. Treatment that includes a third drug, a protease inhibitor, has even stronger results, other studies have shown.

Kit Simpson and colleagues from the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill evaluated the cost of combination therapy in seven countries -- the United States, Australia, Britain, Canada, Germany, Italy and Spain.
Using two drugs together versus AZT alone would save $3,966 or 1,818 pounds per person per year, they said.

John Bartlett and Richard Moore of the Johns Hopkins School of Medicine in Baltimore found costs of AIDS drugs ranged from $185 per month for ddI (Bristol-Myers Squibb's Videx) to $670 per month for ritonavir (Abbott Laboratories' Norvir).
But they said hospitalisation for an AIDS patient in the United States could cost an average of $7,000 per stay.
"The approximate $400 monthly cost of AZT was offset by apparent reduction in the cost of other medical care because of an apparently reduced burden of illness," they reported.
In addition, the drugs can suppress transmission of the virus, which results in even more, hidden savings, they said.
